reference.source: Oxford Handbook of Nephrology and Hypertension / Comprehensive Clinical Nephrology
clinicalPearls: Antenatal (severe neonatal) Bartter syndrome arises from loss-of-function variants affecting the thick ascending limb of the loop of Henle, classically SLC12A1 (encoding the NKCC2 cotransporter, type 1) or KCNJ1 (encoding the ROMK potassium channel, type 2)
It presents before birth with marked polyhydramnios from fetal polyuria, often triggering premature delivery
The biochemical signature is a hypokalaemic, hypochloraemic metabolic alkalosis with salt wasting, high urinary calcium, and grossly elevated plasma renin and aldosterone
Blood pressure is normal or low despite the very high aldosterone, because the underlying defect is renal salt loss rather than mineralocorticoid excess
Nephrocalcinosis frequently develops as a consequence of persistent hypercalciuria
ROMK (type 2) disease may show transient neonatal hyperkalaemia before the characteristic hypokalaemia emerges
Prostaglandin overproduction drives much of the polyuria and systemic features, so a cyclo-oxygenase inhibitor is used to reduce urinary losses, alongside potassium and salt replacement
It functionally mimics chronic loop-diuretic exposure and must be distinguished from surreptitious diuretic use
reference.pathophysiology: Antenatal Bartter syndrome results from inherited loss of salt reabsorption in the thick ascending limb of the loop of Henle, where the NKCC2 cotransporter (SLC12A1) and the apical ROMK channel (KCNJ1) normally drive sodium, potassium and chloride uptake and recycle potassium back into the tubular lumen. When these fail, sodium chloride is lost in the urine, activating the renin-angiotensin-aldosterone system and increasing distal sodium reabsorption in exchange for potassium and hydrogen ion, which produces hypokalaemic metabolic alkalosis. Impaired salt handling also dissipates the transepithelial voltage that normally drives paracellular calcium reabsorption, causing hypercalciuria and nephrocalcinosis. Compensatory renal prostaglandin synthesis amplifies polyuria and systemic vasodilatation, explaining the severe fetal and neonatal phenotype and the benefit of prostaglandin inhibition.
additionalDifferentials: Gitelman syndrome (distal convoluted tubule defect, with hypocalciuria and hypomagnesaemia)
Surreptitious loop or thiazide diuretic use
Chronic vomiting or nasogastric losses causing metabolic alkalosis
Cystic fibrosis with salt loss (pseudo-Bartter presentation)
additionalInvestigations: Serum electrolytes, magnesium and bicarbonate to define the hypokalaemic hypochloraemic alkalosis
Plasma renin and aldosterone (both markedly elevated)
Urinary calcium-to-creatinine ratio and urinary electrolytes to demonstrate salt wasting and hypercalciuria
Renal tract ultrasound looking for nephrocalcinosis
Screening for diuretic use to exclude a factitious cause
Molecular genetic testing of SLC12A1, KCNJ1 and related tubulopathy genes
redFlags: Severe polyhydramnios with threatened extreme prematurity
Life-threatening neonatal dehydration and electrolyte disturbance
Failure to thrive with growth restriction
Progressive nephrocalcinosis with declining renal function
reference.prognosis: With early salt and potassium replacement and prostaglandin inhibition, many children stabilise and grow, though nephrocalcinosis and a degree of chronic kidney impairment may persist. Long-term outcome depends on the genetic subtype and on avoiding recurrent severe electrolyte crises.
pitfalls: Mistaking the presentation for surreptitious diuretic use, or vice versa
Confusing it with Gitelman syndrome, which characteristically causes hypocalciuria and hypomagnesaemia rather than hypercalciuria
Interpreting the very high aldosterone as primary hyperaldosteronism despite normal or low blood pressure
Overlooking transient neonatal hyperkalaemia in ROMK-related disease
Neglecting nephrocalcinosis surveillance and cumulative renal injury
references: Comprehensive Clinical Nephrology (Feehally, Floege, Tonelli, Johnson)
Oxford Handbook of Nephrology and Hypertension
management: Aggressive neonatal sodium chloride, fluid and potassium replacement to counter severe salt wasting and volume depletion
Prostaglandin synthetase inhibition with indometacin to reduce polyuria, salt wasting and the alkalosis
Potassium-sparing diuretics such as spironolactone or amiloride to limit renal potassium losses
Neonatal intensive-care management of prematurity and its complications
Antenatal recognition with monitoring of polyhydramnios and consideration of amnioreduction to reduce preterm labour risk
Surveillance of renal function and growth, with renal ultrasound for nephrocalcinosis
Molecular genetic diagnosis and genetic counselling with family assessment
